title: American Heritage Riverboat Capsizes in New Orleans After Tanker Strike
excerpt: The American Heritage riverboat capsized on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday afternoon after being struck by the tanker Atlantic Asphalt, sending passengers into the water and triggering a major rescue effort.
content:
The American Heritage riverboat capsized on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday afternoon, Nov. 13, after it was struck by the tanker Atlantic Asphalt, sending passengers into the water and triggering a major rescue operation.

The collision happened at about 12:30 p.m. Central Time, below the Crescent City Connection bridge. The Atlantic Asphalt, a Marshall Islands-flagged, 524-foot asphalt and bitumen tanker, struck the riverboat while it was docked.

About 129 passengers were aboard the American Heritage, along with crew members. The riverboat rolled onto its side, capsized and was left partially submerged in the river.

A major rescue is underway, with the U.S. Coast Guard, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, EMS and Port NOLA Harbor Police responding to pull people from the water.

The Mississippi River has been closed to vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96 while the rescue and response continue.

More than a dozen people have been hospitalized, according to WDSU, citing the mayor's office. No deaths have been reported at this time. The cause of the collision is under investigation. This is a developing story.

Update — November 13, 2026

Every passenger and crew member aboard the American Heritage has been accounted for — 195 people in all — and no one was killed, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at an evening news conference, calling the outcome "a miracle on the Mississippi." Thirty-two people were taken to area hospitals — 30 passengers and two New Orleans Harbor Police officers who went into the water during the rescue — and none had critical injuries, the mayor said.

The National Transportation Safety Board has sent a Go Team to the scene, expected to arrive Saturday morning, Nov. 14, to determine what caused the tanker to lose control. The Coast Guard closed about three miles of the Mississippi River, from mile marker 93 to 96, while the response continues. The cause of the collision remains under investigation.

Update — November 14, 2026

The Mississippi River is open to all vessel traffic again, the U.S. Coast Guard told USA Today on Saturday. A 500-foot safety zone remains in effect around the capsized American Heritage. The river had been closed from mile marker 93 to 96 since Friday afternoon, after the tanker Atlantic Asphalt struck the docked riverboat.

American Cruise Lines said Saturday that Captain Leonard Stewart stayed on the bridge as the vessel capsized, calling for aid and keeping the ship alongside the dock for as long as possible. The cause of the collision remains under investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board and the Coast Guard.

Update — November 14, 2026 (evening)

Investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board said Saturday they have recovered the voyage data recorder from the tanker Atlantic Asphalt, which records the ship's speed, direction and course as well as audio from the bridge, Reuters reported. The NTSB has 16 investigators on site and expects to release a preliminary report within 30 days, board member John DeLeeuw said at a Saturday news conference.

The Port of New Orleans filed a federal lawsuit Friday seeking control of the tanker and alleging at least $1 million in damage to its terminal, and a judge issued a warrant giving federal officials control of the vessel for now, the Associated Press reported. The tanker has been towed away from the site.

Eight people remained hospitalized Saturday — two in serious condition and six stable — after 32 people were taken to hospitals following the collision, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at a Saturday briefing. No one was killed. The Coast Guard plans to remove about 16,000 gallons of fuel from the capsized American Heritage before salvage, which officials said could take weeks. The cause of the collision remains under investigation; the Coast Guard said early signs point to a loss of steering on the tanker.
